parts.text: Good morning everyone. We are presenting our in-house project, an AI-based User and Entity Behaviour Analytics system - a security tool that learns how each person in an organisation normally behaves, and raises an alert when someone suddenly behaves out of character.

I'm Tarun Jadhav, and with me is Amaan Saify. We are seventh-semester B.Tech students in Cyber Security, and we did this project under the supervision of Dr. Rathnakar Achary. Let me start with the problem we are solving.

title: Attackers who log in look like employees

parts.text: Most traditional security tools work on signatures: they ask whether something matches a known attack. That works for known malware, but today many breaches start with a stolen password or with an insider. Once an attacker logs in with a real account, everything they do looks legitimate, so signatures don't fire. Behaviour analytics asks a different question: is this normal for this person? For example, a finance user logging in at 2:20 in the morning and reading payroll, someone uploading 3.3 gigabytes to a website they have never used, or a sales account suddenly running admin commands. None of these is malware, but each one is out of character, and those are exactly the cases our system is built to catch.

title: What we set out to build

parts.text: We set four objectives. First, learn: build a personal baseline and a department baseline for every user and every device from their own history. Second, detect: combine statistics, machine learning and threat rules, without needing any labelled examples of attacks, because real organisations almost never have them. Third, explain: every alert must say in plain numbers why it was raised. And fourth, operate: deliver it as a working security console, not just a notebook experiment. It is built in Python with scikit-learn, Streamlit and SQLite, plus a local language model through Ollama.

Before building, we reviewed recent work from IEEE and ACM journals. Graph models like DD-GCN report around 98 percent accuracy on the CERT insider dataset, but they need labelled insiders to train. Most papers profile only users or only hosts, and they output a score without an explanation. One system, Euler, has an excellent AUC of 0.99, yet only 0.6 percent of its alerts are real - almost every alert is false. So the gap is not a better single algorithm. It is combining these techniques into one system that needs no labels, explains itself, controls false alarms, and can actually be run day to day. Amaan will now show how we built it.

title: From raw logs to an explained alert

parts.text: Thank you, Tarun. This is the pipeline. We collect logs - Linux auth logs, Windows event logs including Sysmon, web proxy logs, or any CSV. We normalise them into one common format, and column names are mapped automatically. Then we profile: every day, each user gets 44 behavioural features and each device 19 - things like login hours, new countries, data uploaded, new websites and first-time admin actions. The detection layer scores how unusual each day is, the scores are combined into a risk from 0 to 100, and anything above 45 becomes an alert, grouped into a case. Logs can arrive by upload, a drop folder, a secured API or an endpoint agent, and new data is scored in seconds.

Detection has three layers. The first is behavioural statistics: how far today is from this person's own history and from their department. The second is a machine-learning ensemble of three unsupervised models - Isolation Forest, Local Outlier Factor and a neural-network autoencoder. They are trained only on normal days, so they need no attack labels and can flag attacks they have never seen. The third is 33 threat rules mapped to MITRE ATT&CK, like brute force or clearing the security log. The key design decision is that the threshold is set so one statistic alone can never raise an alert - the ML or a rule has to agree. That is what keeps false alarms low. And suspicious days are never learned as normal, so an attacker cannot slowly train the system.

title: A local language model explains every case

parts.text: On top of detection we added generative AI. A language model, Qwen 2.5 with 7 billion parameters, runs locally through Ollama - no log data ever leaves the machine, which matters for a security tool. With one click it writes a case summary: what happened, how serious it is, and next steps. This is real output for one of our cases. It can also explain a suspicious PowerShell or sudo command. Importantly, the language model only explains - it never decides what is an alert, and text from the logs is fenced off so an attacker cannot hide instructions in a log.

title: A security console analysts can work in

parts.text: Everything comes together in this console. The overview shows alerts per day, the riskiest people and the attack techniques seen. The user activity page shows what a person actually did on a given day - the websites, downloads, blocked attempts, files, USB devices and PowerShell commands - with the out-of-character steps highlighted. So the analyst sees not just a score, but the story. Tarun will walk you through the results.

title: It catches the attacks, with very few false alarms

parts.text: We tested on three datasets. First, a simulated company of 48 people with 12 planted attacks: all 12 were caught on their first day, with an F1 score of 0.95 and on average just one alert per day. Second, a set of raw Linux, Windows and proxy logs with 6 attacks: all 6 were found, and the system read every format by itself. Third - and this is the honest test - the public CERT insider-threat dataset from Carnegie Mellon, which we did not design. There it found 22 of 36 insiders at under one alert a day. The ones it misses are slow, gradual data theft, which we come back to in our limitations.

title: A security tool has to be secure itself

parts.text: A security tool must also be secure itself. Passwords are stored as salted PBKDF2 hashes, five wrong logins lock the account for 15 minutes, and there are three roles - viewer, analyst and admin. API tokens are scoped to one workspace and can be revoked, and every action is recorded in an audit trail. The system has 44 automated tests, including one proving that the fast incremental update gives exactly the same result as re-running everything.

We want to be clear about the limitations. Our main results use a simulated company, which is why we also ran the independent CERT benchmark. Slow, gradual data theft is still mostly missed, because each day on its own looks normal. And some Windows event types, like registry changes, are not analysed yet. For future work, we would add sequence-aware models such as LSTMs or transformers to catch gradual insiders, support more log sources like Microsoft 365, and let the AI assistant answer questions over the data and draft incident reports.
To conclude: our system learns what normal looks like for every user and device without any attack labels, and it catches attacks early with about one alert a day, each one explained.

It reads real Linux, Windows and proxy logs and runs as a working console, where machine learning detects and a local language model explains. Thank you for listening - we are happy to take your questions.
